1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6.name: Four Knights Game
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6.background: Popular among the Open Games in the nineteenth century, the Four Knights had lost ground by the First World War, and it saw a renaissance in the 1990s, since when grandmasters have played it again.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5.strategy: Attacks the knight that guards e5 and asks Black to react. Unlike in the Ruy Lopez, the c3 knight takes the square from White's c-pawn, so there is no broad pawn centre to build, and the game stays even and manoeuvring rather than sharp.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5.name: Four Knights Game: Spanish Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5.background: With 4.d4, one of the two most common continuations of the Four Knights Game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.g3.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop, castle and build up slowly. It leads to a less drawish game than most of the Four Knights, but Black can equalise with a sound central strike.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.g3.name: Four Knights Game: Glek System
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.g3.background: A modern try advocated by Igor Glek.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4.strategy: Opens the centre at once: White removes Black's e-pawn and develops with space and open lines, with the knight already on c3. It is more direct than the quiet lines, but Black develops easily.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4.name: Four Knights Game: Scotch Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4.background: With 4.Bb5, one of the two most common continuations of the Four Knights Game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.a3.strategy: A waiting move: it takes b4 from Black's bishop and passes the turn, hoping for a Four Knights with colours reversed. It develops nothing, so Black can simply take the centre.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.a3.name: Four Knights Game: Gunsberg Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.a3.background: A specialty of the Polish grandmaster Paweł Blehm.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Nd5.strategy: Leaves the e4 pawn undefended on purpose. A Black knight that grabs it wins a pawn or two, but White gets an active position with traps for the unwary; calm development is the safer way to meet it.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Nd5.name: Four Knights Game: Naroditsky Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Nd5.background: A blitz favourite of Daniel Naroditsky. After his death Hikaru Nakamura played it in memoriam against Magnus Carlsen and called for the line to be known by his name.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Nxe5.strategy: Gives a knight for a pawn in the hope of a lead in development and a pawn centre that drives Black's knights back. Black simply takes the knight, keeps the extra piece and can return it on good terms, so the compensation is not enough.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Nxe5.name: Four Knights Game: Halloween Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Nxe5.background: In 1888 Oskar Cordel reported that Leipzig club players used the gambit to dangerous effect; their name for it, the Müller–Schulze Gambit, was a joke in German and did not refer to any real players. The modern name was given by the German player Steffen Jakob, who compared the shock of facing it when prepared for a boring Four Knights to being frightened by a Halloween mask.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.a3 d6.strategy: A solid reply that guards e5 and opens the c8 bishop's diagonal, keeping the position symmetrical. It is a little passive: claiming the centre with a pawn is the more ambitious way to punish the waiting move.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5 Bb4.name: Four Knights Game: Spanish Variation, Double Spanish
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5 Bb4.background: Black's most common reply to 4.Bb5 and the main line today. It has been played by Nigel Short, Michael Adams and Alexei Shirov, among others.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5 Bb4.strategy: Mirrors White's bishop and eyes the c3 knight that guards e4, so Black's pressure matches White's. The position stays symmetrical and solid, a game of manoeuvring in which neither side has an easy edge: the most reliable way to meet the Spanish bishop.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5 Nd4.name: Four Knights Game: Spanish Variation, Rubinstein Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5 Nd4.background: Named after Akiba Rubinstein, and also known as the Rubinstein Countergambit.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5 Nd4.strategy: An unbalancing counterattack: instead of defending c6, the knight moves to d4 and hits the bishop and the f3 knight at once. It leaves e5 loose, but taking it is not as easy as it looks, and Black plays for activity over safety.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5 Bc5.name: Four Knights Game: Spanish Variation, Classical Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5 Bc5.background: Played in the famous game Louis Paulsen against Paul Morphy at the First American Chess Congress in 1857.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5 Bc5.strategy: The classical set-up: the bishop develops towards f2 and gives Black a tactical defence of e5, since taking on c6 and then e5 runs into a strike at f2. The price is a more open game in which White can choose between quiet and sharp play.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5 a6.strategy: Borrows the Ruy Lopez question, but here the c3 knight already guards e4, so White can take on c6 and go after e5. Black has to rely on a forcing tactic to regain the pawn, which makes this a less natural choice than the mirror moves.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4 exd4.name: Four Knights Game: Scotch Variation Accepted
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4 exd4.strategy: Takes the pawn with tempo, as the capture attacks the c3 knight at once. The centre opens and White has to recover the pawn or move the knight, while Black accepts an open game with no weaknesses of its own.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4 Bb4.strategy: Pins the c3 knight against the king, so that e4 loses its defender and Black threatens to take it. The cost is the e5 pawn, which is attacked twice and defended once: White can simply take it, and Black has to prove that the pin and the pressure on e4 pay for it.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.g3 d5.strategy: Strikes at the centre at once: e4 is attacked by the d-pawn and the f6 knight and defended only by the c3 knight, so White has to resolve the tension. Black claims a share of the centre and reaches an equal game, which takes the sting out of the fianchetto plan.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Nxe5 Nxe5.strategy: Takes the knight: Black is a piece up for a pawn and White's compensation is a lead in development. Accepting is the critical reply, since it puts the extra material to the test and leaves White to prove the attack.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.a3 d6 5.h3.name: Four Knights Game: Gunsberg Variation, Provincial Opening
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.a3 d6 5.h3.strategy: A second waiting move, this time taking g4 from Black's bishop so that a pin on the f3 knight never comes. White keeps a flexible, solid set-up, but two prophylactic moves in a row leave Black free to develop as it likes.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5 a6 5.B.name: Four Knights Game: Spanish Variation, Ranken Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5 a6 5.B.strategy: Gives up the bishop pair to double Black's pawns and remove the knight that guards e5. White trades a short-term threat for a lasting structural edge, and the game heads for a quiet middlegame or endgame where the better structure counts.
Recaptures towards the centre, which opens the c8 bishop. Black accepts doubled c-pawns for the bishop pair, but the e5 pawn is no longer defended by a piece and has to be protected by tactics.

Wins the pawn on the surface, but Black gets it back by force with a knight offer and a queen fork. White is left with the better pawn structure, but not an extra pawn; a quieter move keeps more of the structural edge.

The tactical point: the knight takes e4, and if White takes it back the queen forks both white knights from d4. Black regains the pawn, keeps the bishop pair and gets open lines, in return for the doubled c-pawns.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5 Bb4 5..strategy: Gets the king to safety and out of the b4-bishop's diagonal, so a pin on the c3 knight can never become awkward. White keeps the symmetry, and the bishop on b5 keeps leaning on the c6 knight.

Mirrors White once more: Black's king is as safe as White's, and every plan on one side has an equivalent on the other. The game stays balanced and strategic, and the first side to deviate takes on the risk of unbalancing it.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5 Bb4 5..name: Four Knights Game: Spanish Variation, Double Spanish
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5 Bb4 5..strategy: The main line: it supports e4, opens the c1 bishop to g5 where it can pin the f6 knight against the queen, and commits to nothing. White builds a solid position and keeps all the central plans in hand, accepting a slow, strategic game.

Hits the b4 bishop and offers to trade the f6 knight, aiming at a freer game than the quiet build-up. After the knights are exchanged, Black can counter against the f3 knight, so White has to be ready for complications.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5 Bb4 5..name: Four Knights Game: Spanish Variation, Nimzowitsch Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5 Bb4 5..background: Played by Aron Nimzowitsch, it is White's only notable alternative to 6.d3.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5 Bb4 5..strategy: Trades the bishop for the knight to double Black's pawns and loosen e5, aiming for a slightly healthier pawn structure. The cost is the bishop pair, which Black gets along with open lines, so White has to play for the long-term edge.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5 Bb4 5..name: Four Knights Game: Spanish Variation, Symmetrical Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5 Bb4 5..strategy: Mirrors White again: e5 is firmly guarded and the c8 bishop is released. Black keeps the position closed and symmetrical, and White's attempts to create pressure, such as a pin on the f6 knight, are answered in kind. Hard to unbalance, easy to play.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5 Bb4 5..name: Four Knights Game: Spanish Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5 Bb4 5..background: Played by Dawid Janowski, it is Black's main alternative to 6...d6.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5 Bb4 5..strategy: Takes the knight so that White recaptures with doubled c-pawns and an open b-file. Black gives up the bishop pair for the damaged structure, which is a fair trade but not a convincing one: White gets the two bishops and Black has no pressing follow-up.

Backs e5 and the f6 knight with the queen and keeps the pawn structure flexible. But the queen steps onto the diagonal where a bishop on g5 pins the f6 knight against it, so this is less precise than simply mirroring White.

Removes the intruder, which attacks both the b4 bishop and the f6 knight and cannot be left alone. After the recapture the d5 pawn attacks the c6 knight and the e5 pawn needs its support, so Black has to strike in the centre at once.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5 Bc5 5..strategy: Castles into safety and keeps the tactical trick of taking on e5 in reserve, since a pawn fork on d4 would win the material back. A calm choice that leaves Black to say where the game goes.
Castles in turn, which takes the king off the b5 bishop's diagonal and keeps the bishop on c5 aimed at f2. Black has solid development and an equal position, with no weakness for White to attack.

The central fork trick: after Black recaptures, a pawn thrust attacks bishop and knight at once, and the material comes back level. White wins no pawn, but gains space and trades into a symmetrical, drawish game.
The natural recapture. White's pawn fork then hits both the bishop and the knight, so Black has to trade down and reaches an equal, simplified game with no real risk.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5 Nd4 5..strategy: Keeps the bishop and the pressure on the c6 square, and asks Black to justify the knight's adventure. It is the most common reply: White avoids the exchanges and leaves Black to find compensation with a gambit.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5 Nd4 5..name: Four Knights Game: Spanish Variation, Rubinstein Variation Accepted
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5 Nd4 5..strategy: Takes the knight at once, so Black recaptures with the pawn and the d4 pawn hits the c3 knight. The position simplifies into a wholesale exchange, solid for White but very drawish, and it discourages ambitious Black players from the whole line.

Grabs the pawn, but cannot keep it: Black's queen comes to e7 with an attack on the knight while the bishop is still hit by the knight on d4, so White loses time and the pawn goes back. Black gets the bishop pair as compensation.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5 Nd4 5..name: Four Knights Game: Spanish Variation, Rubinstein Variation, Henneberger Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5 Nd4 5..strategy: Castles and ignores the knight on d4, declining both the trade and the pawn grab. It is calm and safe, but Black can trade the knight for the bishop at leisure, so the early excursion yields little and White gains no advantage.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5 Nd4 5..name: Four Knights Game: Spanish Variation, Rubinstein Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5 Nd4 5..strategy: Steps out of the knight's way to the most passive square: the bishop gives up its pressure on c6, and Black can trade the active knight for White's f3 knight with an easy game. Harmless, but it wastes the time spent on the bishop.

Develops and prepares to gambit the e5 pawn: the bishop supports the d4 knight and eyes f2, trading a pawn for fast development and a grip on the centre. Black plays for activity and has to prove it is enough.
Trades the active knight for the one on f3, with check. White has spent two moves on the bishop for nothing, so Black has no problems, and the trade takes the sting out of White's slow set-up.

Wins the pawn back: the queen attacks the loose e5 knight while the d4 knight hits the bishop, and once the knights are traded on b5 the queen takes e4 with check. Black regains the pawn and keeps the bishop pair, which is why the grab is not dangerous.

Develops instead of regaining the pawn at once. The bishop backs the d4 knight and aims at f2, but the e5 knight is not attacked, so White keeps the extra pawn for now and Black must find a follow-up.

Accepts the gambit and takes the pawn. White now has to consolidate against Black's lead in development, usually by retreating the knight with a hit on the bishop, and cannot relax until the pieces are safely developed.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5 Nd4 5..name: Four Knights Game: Spanish Variation, Rubinstein Variation, Marshall Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5 Nd4 5..strategy: Castles instead of recovering the pawn: Black sacrifices e5 for development, relying on the active knight on d4 and bishop on c5. A real gambit, so Black has to show that the activity is worth the pawn.
The natural recapture: the bishop keeps the e4 pawn defended and White's centre intact. The game is equal and quiet, and neither side has a clear plan.
Develops with an eye on f2 and gets the bishop to the best diagonal. Black has equal chances and an easy development, and White's two spent bishop moves leave nothing to attack.

Castles at once, putting the king away and a rook on f1 to guard f2, where the c5 bishop aims from behind its own d4 knight. White keeps the extra pawn for the moment and accepts a sharp game, since the d4 knight attacks the b5 bishop, which only the c3 knight covers.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5 Nd4 5..name: Four Knights Game: Spanish Variation, Rubinstein Variation, Marshall Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5 Nd4 5..strategy: Castles in turn and bets on activity against the pawn it is down: the d4 knight attacks the b5 bishop, the f6 knight presses on e4 and the c5 bishop lines up on f2. White's e5 knight stays, so Black has to make that piece activity count.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5 Nd4 5..name: Four Knights Game: Spanish Variation, Rubinstein Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5 Nd4 5..strategy: Holds the e5 knight with a pawn so that White keeps the extra pawn, at the price of loosening the king's side and the e1-h4 diagonal. Black can trade on b5 and undermine the knight, regaining the pawn because the knight leaves e4 unprotected.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4 Bb4 5.N.name: Four Knights Game: Scotch Variation, Krause Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4 Bb4 5.N.strategy: Wins the e5 pawn, with the knight supported by the d4 pawn. It is a real gambit all the same: the pinned c3 knight leaves e4 short of defenders, so White takes the pawn at the price of quick counterplay against the centre and the exposed knights.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4 Bb4 5.d.strategy: Drives the c6 knight away with a gain of space and leaves the e5 pawn undefended. The fight moves from the pawn to the centre: White has more room, Black has the pin on c3 and the loose e4 pawn to work with.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4 Bb4 5.d.name: Four Knights Game: Scotch Variation, Oxford Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4 Bb4 5.d.strategy: Moves the attacked knight to the centre, where the e5 pawn guards it and where it eyes f3 and c2. Black gives up the e5 pawn for this, which White can take, and relies on the pin and the pressure on e4 and f3 for compensation.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4 Bb4 5.N.name: Four Knights Game: Scotch Variation, Krause Gambit, Leonhardt Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4 Bb4 5.N.strategy: Attacks the e5 knight a second time, so that the c6 knight and the queen together outweigh the d4 pawn that guards it, and brings the queen to the e-file. White cannot keep the extra pawn without finding more support for the knight.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..strategy: Recovers the pawn and puts the knight on a central square, defended by the queen, from where it eyes c6. White gets the open game it wanted, with simple development and the chance to trade on c6 and damage Black's pawn structure.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..name: Four Knights Game: Scotch Variation, Belgrade Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..background: The first recorded game in this line was played between Kurt Richter and Albert Becker in Berlin in 1938. The association with Belgrade comes from the 1945 Belgrade championship, where it was played by Mihailo Trajkovic against Miroslav Radojcic.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..strategy: Sidesteps the attack by jumping forward and offers the e4 pawn in return for quick piece play. Black has several sound ways to take or decline and, with accurate play, equalises, so White gets practical chances at the price of a pawn.
Takes the offered pawn and keeps it for now, a sharp way to meet the gambit. Black asks White to show real compensation, since White's lead in development is all there is to pay for the pawn.

Pins the c3 knight and with it the defence of e4, while the c6 knight attacks the d4 knight, which only the queen guards. White cannot calmly defend the pawn and usually trades on c6 first. A natural main line that leaves Black with a sound, flexible game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..name: Four Knights Game: Scotch Variation, Schmid Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..strategy: A temporary knight sacrifice: when White takes on e4, the queen pins that knight to the king and the c6 knight attacks the d4 knight, so Black wins the piece back. Material comes out equal in an open, unbalanced position that asks Black to know the follow-up.

Pins the e4 knight to the king and attacks it, with nothing yet defending it, while the d5 knight adds pressure around c7. Black has to defend at once and accurately; the move is the sharpest test of the pawn grab.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..name: Four Knights Game: Scotch Variation, Belgrade Gambit, Modern Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..strategy: Defends the pinned knight with a pawn and so keeps the extra pawn. The price is a weakened kingside and an open diagonal from the king, and the pin is still there, so Black has to meet White's piece play with care.

Trades off the knight that attacks d4, with tempo, since the capture also attacks the queen. White removes the target before the bishop defends e4 and forces Black to double the c-pawns, a structural concession that ...d5 can later repair.
Recaptures towards the centre and keeps the queens on, which the other recapture would not. The doubled c-pawns are a weakness, but Black gets an open b-file and can undouble them with ...d5.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.g3 d5 5.ex.strategy: Resolves the tension by capturing, since e4 is attacked twice and defended once. The centre opens before the bishop reaches g2, and White prepares to use the long diagonal later in a game of quick development.

Recaptures with the knight, which settles on a central square and attacks the c3 knight. Black's pieces become active, the d-pawn is gone from the centre, and Black has to be ready to meet the pressure White builds with the fianchetto.

Puts the bishop on the long diagonal, the point of the g3 set-up, behind the f3 knight, and prepares castling. White accepts a quiet game and pressure on the centre and the queenside from a distance, instead of occupying it.

Trades off White's knight on c3. Either recapture doubles White's c-pawns, though it opens the b-file or the d-file for White. Black simplifies and eases the game, at the price of letting the g2 bishop work freely.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Nxe5 Nxe5.strategy: The point of the gambit: the pawn attacks the e5 knight with tempo and White builds a broad centre with the e-pawn. White hopes to drive the black knights back and make the lead in development count before Black can untangle.

Goes back to c6, where it attacks the d4 pawn and stays in the centre. It keeps the extra piece and leaves Black with more good answers to White's space-gaining pawn moves than the retreat to the edge.

Retreats to g6, out of the pawn's reach, and keeps the piece. The knight is awkwardly placed and the f6 knight can be chased back, so Black spends time to hold the material, with a solid game if it consolidates.

Chases the c6 knight again with a pawn, gaining space at the cost of time. White keeps the gambit going and plays for speed instead of material, but the pawn on d5 is also a target and Black has good ways to meet the attack.

Jumps back to e5 and keeps the piece, but the knight can be chased again and White's central pawns gain more space with each move. Black's pieces are pushed about and White's attack is dangerous in practice, so the defence has to be exact.

Drives the f6 knight back with the pawn, gaining space and time. White's central pawns and lead in development are the compensation for the piece; if Black consolidates safely, White is simply a piece down.

Retreats all the way home and keeps the extra piece, but undoes Black's development, so White's pawns dominate the centre. Black has to catch up in development without falling into tactics, and may return the material for a calmer game.
